claims.text: A two-phase coexistence simulation combined with a machine-learning interatomic potential can determine the melting temperature of refractory alloys.
The approach can determine the enthalpy of fusion of refractory alloys.
The approach can determine the entropy of fusion of refractory alloys.
The approach can determine the volume change at melting for refractory alloys.
The proposed approach has a much lower computational cost than full ab initio thermodynamic integration.
The machine-learning potential reproduces DFT-level interatomic forces accurately.
Using a machine-learning potential permits larger-scale and longer-timescale molecular-dynamics simulations than direct ab initio simulation.
Equilibration of coexisting solid and liquid regions yields the melting temperature.
Latent heat can be extracted from the coexistence simulation.
Entropy of fusion can be derived from the latent heat at the melting temperature.
Volume change at melting can be extracted directly from the coexistence simulation.
The solid-liquid coexistence interface mediates the free-energy balance at melting.
The method should predict the specified melting properties to roughly within 10% of full ab initio or experimental results.
The reduced computational cost would enable higher-throughput screening of refractory systems.
DFT-based thermodynamic-integration calculations are accurate for melting-property prediction.
DFT-based thermodynamic integration is prohibitively expensive for high-throughput studies.
Prediction accuracy depends on the quality and transferability of the machine-learning potential.
Extreme anharmonicity near melting can limit the precision of the method.
Chemical complexity can limit the precision of the method.
